name: Persian Constitutional Revolution
info: The Persian Constitutional Revolution, also called the Constitutional Revolution of Iran, was the movement of 1905 to 1911 under the Qajar dynasty that won Iran a parliament and a constitution and ended with the expulsion of the Second Majlis.

facts.where: Iran (Persia): Tehran, Tabriz, Rasht, Qazvin, Isfahan and other cities, with the Shi'i schools of Najaf in Iraq giving rulings from outside.
facts.period: Protest against the customs director and the shah's loans (1905); the shah's agreement to a house of justice (January 1906) and to a parliament (August 1906); the first Majlis (from October 1906); the Minor Tyranny and civil war (1908–1909); the second constitutional period (1909–1911); the expulsion of the deputies of the Second Majlis (December 1911).
facts.figures: Mozaffar ad-Din Shah Qajar and Mohammad Ali Shah Qajar; the clerics Akhund Khurasani, Mirza Husayn Tehrani, Shaykh Abdullah Mazandarani, Sayyed Mohammad Tabatabai and Fazlollah Nouri; the Tabriz commanders Sattar Khan and Bagher Khan; Yeprem Khan; the American lawyer William Morgan Shuster.
facts.outcome: A parliament with final approval of loans and the budget, and a constitution that lasted, though not adhered to, until 1979; but also the Anglo-Russian division of the country in 1907, the shelling of the Majlis in 1908, and the expulsion of the Second Majlis in 1911 with the support of 12,000 Russian troops.

t: A coalition of the ulama, liberal and radical intellectuals and the bazaar forced the Qajar shah to accept a parliament in 1906, though the three groups were united by common enemies rather than common goals.
Clerics were on both sides: Akhund Khurasani and two other leading marja' in Najaf backed the constitution, while Fazlollah Nouri opposed it and was hanged in July 1909.
Constitutionalists restored the constitution in 1909 after the Minor Tyranny, but the revolution ended in December 1911 when the Second Majlis was expelled with the support of 12,000 Russian troops.
dyk: The tobacco protest of 1891 to 1892 worked so well that Iranians stopped smoking despite their love of tobacco, and it was said that even the women of the shah's harem gave it up.
ev: The tobacco protest begins against a 50-year monopoly granted to an Englishman, and Mirza Hasan Shirazi's fatwa of December 1891 closes the bazaars and stops the smoking of tobacco
Merchants and clergy protest against tariffs imposed to repay the Russian loan for the shah's tour of Europe
Mozaffar ad-Din Shah agrees to a parliament, and the National Consultative Assembly first meets in October
The Anglo-Russian Convention divides Iran into a Russian zone in the north and a British zone in the south
Mohammad Ali Shah stages a coup and bombards the parliament, beginning the Minor Tyranny
Constitutionalist forces march on Tehran, force the shah to abdicate and re-establish the constitution; Fazlollah Nouri is hanged in July
Sattar Khan refuses to disarm and is wounded in a confrontation with Yeprem Khan, the police chief of Tehran
In December the shah's cabinet, backed by 12,000 Russian troops, expels the deputies of the Second Majlis

sections.background:
In the late 19th century Iran, like most of the Muslim world, suffered from foreign intrusion and exploitation, military weakness, lack of cohesion and corruption. By the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813 and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 it lost Georgia, Armenia and its Caspian navy to Russia and paid an indemnity of three million pounds to the tsar; in the Treaty of Paris of 1857 it agreed to withdraw from Herat. The Qajar shahs had no standing army, relying on tribal contingents, and sold titles, patents, concessions, monopolies and lands, spending part of the proceeds on the court. Mass-manufactured foreign textiles undermined the traditional handicrafts: in Isfahan not even a fifth of the weavers' guilds survived the competition, and by 1894 the price farmers were paid for wheat had fallen to a sixth of its 1871 level.

A concession of 1872 gave a British citizen control over roads, telegraphs, mills, factories and mining in exchange for a fixed sum and 60% of net revenue; it was rolled back after bitter local opposition. In March 1890 Naser al-Din Shah granted Baron Paul Julius Reuter a 50-year tobacco monopoly. Protest spread first among the bazaari and then the ulama, and in December 1891 the marja'-e taqlid Mirza Hasan Shirazi declared the use of tobacco tantamount to war against the Hidden Imam. Nikki Keddie traced a direct line from the coalition of the tobacco protest to the Constitutional Revolution. The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–05 and the Russian revolution of 1905 gave further impetus, as constitutions came to be seen as the secret of Western strength.
sections.aims:
The constitutionalist movement rested on an alliance of the ulama, liberal and radical intellectuals and the bazaar, an alliance based on common enemies rather than common goals. The ulama sought to extend their own power and to have Shi'i Islam more strictly enforced; the liberals and radicals wanted greater political and social democracy and economic development; and the bazaaris wanted to restrict the favoured economic status of foreigners and their competition. The intellectuals were a small but growing group, many of whom had learned of Western ways while travelling abroad and were struck by Western economic development, comparative justice and lack of arbitrary rule. In their writings they criticised autocratic rulers, petty officials, venal clerics, arbitrary courts and the low status of women.

The bazaari became convinced that law and order, security of property and immunity from arbitrary power could all be achieved by importing parliamentary democracy from Europe. The ulama had less to gain, but were convinced for a time that their position beside the monarchy would not be weakened. The revolutionaries argued that Iran's oil industry was being sold to the British, that tax breaks on imports, exports and manufactured textiles were destroying an economy sustained by the bazaar merchants, and that the shah was selling assets to pay interest on his foreign debt. The concrete demand became a parliament, a majlis, that would limit the power of the shah.
sections.events:
In 1905 protests arose over tariffs imposed to repay the Russian loan that had financed Mozaffar ad-Din Shah's tour of Europe. In December two Tehran merchants were bastinadoed for price-gouging, the merchants closed the bazaar and the clergy followed. The government dispersed protesters who had taken sanctuary in a mosque, and a larger movement took refuge at a shrine outside Tehran. On 12 January 1906 the shah agreed to dismiss his prime minister and transfer power to a house of justice. In a later fight government forces killed a sayyid, and Cossacks killed 22 protesters and injured 100; the ulama went on strike and many merchants took shelter at the British embassy. In the summer of 1906 about 12,000 men camped in its gardens, and the shah agreed to a parliament in August. The National Consultative Assembly, with 156 members elected mostly from Tehran and the merchant class, met in October; the constitution was modelled in part on that of Belgium.

Mohammad Ali Shah, who opposed the constitution, came to power in January 1907, and in August the Anglo-Russian Convention divided Iran into zones. In 1908 the shah staged a coup and bombarded the parliament, a time called the Minor Tyranny. Rebels held out in Tabriz under Sattar Khan and by April 1909 had driven out the royalist forces. Constitutionalists marched on Tehran, forced the shah to abdicate in favour of his young son Ahmad Shah and restored the constitution in 1909.
sections.people:
The clergy were divided. Three of the highest-ranking marja' of the time, Akhund Khurasani, Mirza Husayn Tehrani and Shaykh Abdullah Mazandarani, telegraphed fatwas in favour of the constitution from Najaf. Khurasani and his student Muhammad Hossain Naini argued that complete justice was impossible until the return of the Hidden Imam, but that democracy reduces the tyranny of the state and was a lesser evil that Shi'i Muslims must support. Sayyed Mohammad Tabatabai and Sayyed Abdullah Behbahani were the two most widely recognised clerical leaders in Iran itself. Mohammed Kazem Yazdi stayed neutral most of the time, though he reviewed the draft constitution, suggested changes and signed it.

Fazlollah Nouri led the opponents. He held that sharia was a complete code of life and that any other code was unnecessary and against Islam, and he told Shi'i Muslims to ignore the marja' they followed if that marja' supported democracy. Supporters named him a court official with a vested interest in the old order who had ties to the Russians. Nouri began a sit-in at the Shah Abdol-Azim Shrine on 21 June 1907 that lasted until 16 September 1907. The commanders of the Tabriz resistance were Sattar Khan and his lieutenant Bagher Khan; Armenian leaders such as Yeprem Khan and Khetcho took part, as did the American teacher Howard Baskerville, who was killed. The Bakhtiyari leaders joined the Tabriz rebels, and Sardar Assad's forces captured Tehran in 1909. Vladimir Liakhov, a Russian colonel, commanded the Persian Cossack Brigade that shelled parliament.
sections.outcomes:
The revolution produced a parliament with final approval of all loans and the budget. The fundamental laws of 30 December 1906 provided for a National Consultative Assembly and a Senate, and the Constitutional Amendment of 1907 declared Twelver Shi'ism the state religion and called for a council of five high-ranking Twelver Shia clerics to ensure that parliament's laws did not contradict the laws of Islam. The electoral law of 9 September 1906 excluded women, foreigners, men under 25 and others from voting. The constitution, though not adhered to, remained in force until after the Islamic Revolution.

Violence marked the struggle on both sides. In Zanjan Mulla Qurban Ali Zanjani is reported to have mobilised six hundred men who looted the shops of pro-democracy merchants and killed the representative Sa'd al-Saltanih. After the march on Tehran a Revolutionary Tribunal found Nouri guilty of inciting mobs and of issuing fatwas that declared parliamentary leaders apostates whose blood ought to be shed, and in July 1909 he was hanged as a traitor. The movement then split: in 1910 Sattar Khan refused an order to disarm and was wounded when Yeprem Khan, the police chief of Tehran, disarmed his fighters.

The revolution ended in December 1911, when the deputies of the Second Majlis, weakened by internal dissension, the apathy of the masses, the antagonism of the upper class and the open enmity of Britain and Russia, were roughly expelled and threatened with death if they returned by the shah's cabinet, backed by 12,000 Russian troops.
sections.legacy:
The legacy of the revolution in Iran is mixed. It has been called an epoch-making episode in the modern history of Persia and the first of its kind in the Islamic world, earlier than the Young Turk revolution of 1908. It opened the way for debate in a burgeoning press and for new institutions in place of the old order. After the 1921 coup, parliament amended the constitution on 12 December 1925, replacing the Qajar dynasty with the Pahlavi dynasty as the legitimate sovereigns of Iran. The 1906–1907 constitution remained until a new one was approved in a referendum on 2 and 3 December 1979 that established an Islamic republic.

Ruhollah Khomeini, leader of the 1979 revolution, who was a child at the time, held that the constitution of 1906 was the work of agents of imperialist Britain, who he said had borrowed a Belgian legal code and added some ordinances of Islam in order to deceive the people. After the Iranian revolution Nouri was celebrated enough in the Islamic Republic to have an expressway named after him, though he had defended the monarchy against the constitution. Reza Aslan argues that what separates the uprisings of 1906, 1953 and 1979 that resulted in radical change from the countless others of the last hundred-odd years is a coalition of the educated middle class, the mid-level clerics and seminary students, and the bazaari merchants.

summary: The Persian Constitutional Revolution of 1905 to 1911 brought Iran a parliament and a constitution through an alliance of clerics, intellectuals and bazaar merchants against the Qajar shah. It survived a royal coup in 1908 but ended when the Second Majlis was expelled in 1911 with the support of Russian troops.
references: Janet Afary, The Iranian Constitutional Revolution, 1906-1911: Grassroots Democracy, Social Democracy, & the Origins of Feminism (Columbia University Press, 1996)
Mangol Bayat, Iran's Experiment with Parliamentary Governance: The Second Majles, 1909-1911 (Syracuse University Press, 2020)
Mansour Bonakdarian, Britain and the Iranian Constitutional Revolution of 1906-1911: Foreign Policy, Imperialism, and Dissent (Syracuse University Press, 2006)
Houri Berberian, Armenians and the Iranian Constitutional Revolution of 1905-1911: The Love for Freedom Has No Fatherland (Routledge, 2018)
Edward G. Browne, The Persian Constitutional Movement (British Academy, 1918)
notes: The article contradicts itself on when the shah signed the constitution: one place says he signed shortly before he died on 8 January 1907, another that he signed by 31 December 1906 and died three days later, and a third dates the proclamation to 5 August 1906 and the fundamental laws to 30 December 1906. The profile gives the August 1906 agreement and the 30 December fundamental laws and avoids a signing date or death date.
The article dates the Russian-backed coup against the Majlis to 1907 in one place and 1908 in another; 1908 is used, as in its Minor Tyranny section and introduction.

The article says the Russian ultimatum over William Morgan Shuster led to the occupation of Tabriz and sets this before the 1909 events, which does not fit the dates it gives elsewhere; Shuster is named only in the facts and not placed in the narrative.
References are copied from the article's Further reading, for the editor to choose from; Kasravi, Foran, Ansari and Nejad were left out (Persian-language or journal items).

The article's claim that Nouri's 'fanaticism' was reinforced by his ties to the court is a verdict of its own and was left out; his ties and the criticisms made of him are reported as his critics' view. The 'Tobacco protest' dates are given as February 1891–January 1892 in one place and a December 1891 fatwa in another; both are used as stated.
Left out as thin or unsourced detail: the lists of notable participants beyond those with a stated role; the quoted fatwas, whose texts the saved article does not contain.
The article says the first elections gave 156 members 'the overwhelming majority from Tehran and the merchant class'; kept as given.
Zanjani's six hundred 'thugs' is the article's word; the profile says 'men' and 'is reported to have'.
